what_it_does: Modern AI models that generate 3D video must pay close attention to every part of every frame at every moment, and this 'attention' computation (the process where the model weighs how relevant each pixel or patch is to every other) can eat up more than three-quarters of the total processing time and energy. The authors noticed that adjacent video frames are often very similar to each other, and that many regions within a frame repeat or resemble each other closely — an insight borrowed from decades of classical video compression research. SimPicker is a combined software-and-chip co-design that exploits this similarity: at a coarse level it speculates which entire frames can be partially skipped, and at a fine level it finds matching small patches (tokens) within a frame using a fast lookup table built into the chip. To handle the fact that similar patches are scattered unpredictably across the image, the design also includes an adaptive grouping strategy that batches these irregular workloads into balanced chunks so no part of the chip sits idle. The net effect is lower latency and lower energy for 3D video generation without changing the model's outputs.
